Solitaire in Two Colors

ParityInvariantsLogic

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)

Game: Remove neighbouring cards of the same parity — two odds or two evens — until the circle is empty.
How to play: Click the pink dot between two neighbours. Red cards come from one half of the deck and blue cards from the other.

Look for the math

This game is a magic trick. Two spectators each take half a deck, shuffle it, and the halves are dealt alternately round a circle — red cards from one half, blue from the other. Remove neighbouring cards of the same parity, and the circle closes up. The trick is that for the right deck size you cannot lose, no matter which legal pair you take.

The deal

The numbers 1 to N are split in half: red cards are 1 to N/2, blue cards are N/2 + 1 to N. Each half is shuffled on its own, then the halves are interleaved, so every red card has blue cards on both sides. N is even and between 4 and 40. Every pair you can click is therefore one red card and one blue card.

Two numbers that never move

Count four kinds of card: odd red, odd blue, even red, even blue. Removing two odd neighbours takes one odd red and one odd blue, so the difference

OrOb = (odd red) − (odd blue)

does not change. The same is true of the evens:

ErEb = (even red) − (even blue)

These two differences are the game's invariant. Removing a pair also keeps red and blue alternating: the two cards on the far side of the removed pair were one red and one blue, and they become neighbours.

Why the trick cannot fail

When N is a multiple of 4, each half contains equally many odds and evens. So OrOb = 0 and ErEb = 0 before play, and they stay 0. Now suppose the game got stuck with cards left. Every neighbour would then have the opposite parity, so the parities would alternate all the way round, and the colours would too. That puts every odd card in one colour and every even card in the other, so |OrOb| + |ErEb| would equal the number of cards left — not 0. That contradicts the invariant. A stuck position is impossible, so every line of play ends with an empty circle.

When the magic needs the right choice

If N is even but not a multiple of 4, the two halves are not balanced. With 6 cards, red is 1, 2, 3 and blue is 4, 5, 6: there are two odd reds but only one odd blue, and one even red but two even blues. So OrOb = 1 and ErEb = −1. A stuck position is now possible, and some sequences lose. The game becomes a real puzzle: choose pairs that do not leave the circle alternating in both colour and parity.

The logic test checks the claim by brute force: every shuffle of 4, 6, 8 and 10 cards, and every line of play from it. The sides divisible by 4 always win; every shuffle of 6 or 10 cards has a losing line. For 12, 16, 20 and 40 cards it plays sampled shuffles and confirms each can be won. So the small cases support exactly what the invariant proves.

Try 16 cards and remove any pair you like: the magic trick holds. Then try 6 or 10 and look for the pair that strands the circle — the status line will tell you when there is no legal pair left.
